Most people who say "I am not creative" are really saying "nobody showed me the rules". Good design is mostly a set of simple rules that professional designers apply again and again. In this lesson you learn six of them. Three of them, **contrast, alignment and hierarchy**, will fix most of the flyers you see on WhatsApp statuses and church notice boards.
A woman thinking through a design layout
Design is a set of choices you can learn, not a gift you are born with.
Rule 1: Hierarchy, decide what is read first

**Hierarchy** means arranging things so the eye reads them in the order you want. The most important thing should be the biggest, boldest or most colourful. The second most important thing is smaller. Small details, such as a phone number or address, come last and smallest. If everything is the same size, the viewer does not know where to start, so she scrolls past.

A useful habit: before you open Canva, write your message in three levels on paper. Level 1 is the hook ("Fresh Zobo, 500 naira"). Level 2 is the support ("Chilled, no preservatives, delivery in Ikeja"). Level 3 is the action ("WhatsApp 0803 000 0000"). Each level then gets its own size.
Rule 2: Contrast, make it readable

**Contrast** is the difference between two things: dark against light, big against small, bold against thin. Text must contrast strongly with its background. Yellow text on a white background, or dark blue text on a black background, disappears on a phone screen, especially outdoors in bright sunlight. The international web accessibility guideline (WCAG) asks for a contrast ratio of at least **4.5 to 1** for normal text and **3 to 1** for large text. You do not need to calculate it: free tools such as the WebAIM contrast checker do it for you, and the simple test is to squint. If the words blur into the background when you squint, the contrast is too low.
Rule 3: Alignment, line things up

**Alignment** means every item lines up with something else: the left edge, the centre line, or another block of text. Randomly placed text looks amateur even when the colours are beautiful. Canva helps you here: when you drag an item, thin pink or purple guide lines appear when it lines up with the centre or with another element. Pick one alignment for a design (all left, or all centred) and stick to it. Left alignment is easier to read for more than two lines.
Rules 4 to 6: Repetition, proximity and white space
**Repetition**: use the same two fonts and the same colours across all your posts so people recognise you before they read your name.
**Proximity**: keep related things close together. Price next to product name. Date, time and venue grouped in one block.

**White space**: the empty space around items. It is not wasted. It gives the eye a rest and makes the main message stand out. A good rule is to keep at least a thumb's width of margin around the edge of a phone design.

Building your brand look: colours, fonts and a simple logo

A **brand visual identity** is the set of colours, fonts, logo and photo style that makes people recognise your business before they read your name. Big companies spend a lot on it, but a small business can build a clean one in an afternoon with a phone. The goal is **consistency**: the same look on your flyers, Instagram posts, WhatsApp catalogue, price list and shop sign.
A person choosing colours from a palette
A small, fixed palette makes every post look like it came from the same business.
Step 1: Decide how you want people to feel

Write three words that describe your business personality. A children's tutoring centre might choose "playful, safe, bright". A bridal makeup artist might choose "elegant, soft, premium". A catering business might choose "warm, generous, fresh". These words guide every colour and font choice that follows.
Step 2: Build a palette with HEX codes

Every digital colour has a **HEX code**: a hash sign followed by six letters and numbers, such as #D4006A for a deep magenta. HEX codes let you use exactly the same colour in Canva, CapCut and anywhere else. A practical small palette has:
**One main colour** that people will remember you by.
**One accent colour** for buttons, prices and highlights. It should contrast clearly with the main colour.
**One dark neutral** (near black or dark grey) for body text.
**One light neutral** (white, cream or very light grey) for backgrounds.
Optionally, one extra supporting colour.

Canva has a free colour palette generator on its website, and inside the editor you can tap any colour swatch and type a HEX code. If you already have a logo or a product photo you love, upload it: Canva will show the colours used in that photo under **Photo colours**, and you can copy them.
Step 3: Pair two fonts

Fonts come in families. **Serif** fonts have small feet at the ends of letters (like Playfair Display) and feel classic. **Sans serif** fonts have no feet (like Montserrat or Open Sans) and are very clear on screens. **Script** fonts look like handwriting and are hard to read in long text. A safe pairing is a strong heading font plus a plain sans serif body font. Use script fonts only for one or two decorative words, never for phone numbers or prices.

Two practical font rules for phone screens: body text on a 1080 pixel wide post should rarely be smaller than about 28 to 32 points in Canva, or it becomes hard to read on a small phone; and never use more than two font families in one design. You can still vary weight (regular, bold) and size inside those two families to create hierarchy.
Step 5: Decide your photo style

Your photos are part of your brand too. Decide a simple rule and keep to it, for example "bright daylight photos on a plain cream background" or "people using the product, outdoors, warm light". Mixing dark, yellow-tinted night photos with bright daylight ones makes a feed look untidy even when the colours and fonts match.
Step 4: A simple logo you can own

For most small businesses, a clean **wordmark** (your business name set in your heading font, in your main colour, maybe with one simple shape) is enough. Be careful: Canva's content licence does not allow you to register a trademark for a logo built from Canva's stock graphics or templates, because those elements are not exclusively yours. If you may ever want to register your brand, build the logo from text and basic shapes only, or hire a designer to create original artwork.

Once you know the basics, speed becomes your next goal. A small business owner does not have hours to design every post. In this lesson you set up Canva so that your brand look is built in, and you create a few **master designs** you can reuse every week.
Design tools arranged on a screen

Brand Kit: your colours and fonts in one place

Canva's **Brand Kit** (found under Brand on the home screen or in the menu) stores your logo, colours and fonts so they appear at the top of every colour and font menu. The full Brand Kit, with logos, multiple palettes and uploaded fonts, is a Canva Pro feature, and what the free plan includes has changed over time, so check what your account shows. If you are on the free plan and cannot save a kit, use two workarounds:
Keep a design called "Brand guide" open in a second tab and copy elements from it.
After you use a colour once in a design, Canva shows it under **Document colours**, so set your colours early in each design and they stay one tap away.
Make a master template

Instead of starting from Canva's templates every time, make your own. Design one post you are proud of, then **duplicate** it (tap the three dots on the design in Projects and choose Make a copy) every time you need a new one. Keep the layout, fonts and colours; only change the words and the photo. This is how big brands keep every post consistent.
Good master templates for a small business include: a product post, a price list, a customer review post, a "we are open" or "new stock" announcement, and a story with a question sticker space.
Resizing for different platforms

Canva Pro has a **Resize** feature (Canva calls the newer version Magic Switch) that copies your design into new sizes in one tap. On the free plan, you can do it by hand: create a new design at the new size, then copy and paste elements across from the original. Either way, always check the result, because text near the edges may be cut off or need moving.

Portrait posts at 1080 x 1350 take up more of the screen in the feed than squares, so many creators prefer them for product photos. Stories disappear after 24 hours unless you save them as **Highlights** on your profile, which is a good place to keep a permanent price list or "How to order" story.
The anatomy of a strong feed post
**One message per post.** A post about your new hair braiding style should not also announce your church programme.
**A hook in large text**, five to eight words: "Knotless braids, ready in 4 hours".
**A real photo** of your product or work, sharp and well lit. Real work builds trust faster than stock photos.
**Your brand colours and logo**, small, in the same corner every time.
**A call to action (CTA)**: what should she do now? "Send DM to book", "Tap the link in bio", "WhatsApp 0803 000 0000".
Carousels that people swipe

A carousel works like a mini lesson or catalogue. Slide 1 is the cover: a strong promise such as "5 ways to keep your wig fresh". Slides 2 to 6 deliver one point each, with large text. The last slide is your CTA and contact. In Canva, design all slides as pages in one design, keep the same layout on every page, and download all pages as PNG. Then select them together when you post. Design a small arrow or the words "Swipe" on slide 1 so people know there is more.

Captions that do the selling

Only the first line or two of a caption shows before "more", so put the most important words first. A simple caption formula is **Hook, Value, Proof, Action**. Use short lines and two or three relevant emojis at most. Add a few specific hashtags that real customers might search, such as your city and service (#AbujaCaterer, #LagosMakeupArtist), rather than thirty general ones.

Caption body: three short lines on what is in it (only shea butter and coconut oil), the size (250 g), and the price (3,500 naira).

The post has one clear message, a real photo, and a caption that answers price, size and how to order, which are the three questions customers ask most.
Facebook differences

Facebook uses the same square and portrait sizes, and posts made for Instagram usually work there too. Facebook audiences in Nigeria often include older customers and community groups, so posts with clear prices, location and phone numbers do well. Facebook also lets you post into **groups** you belong to, such as a local buy and sell group; read each group's rules first, because many allow selling posts only on certain days.
After you post

Reply to comments and messages quickly, ideally within a few hours, because a fast reply often decides whether a customer buys from you or the next seller. On a professional or creator account, open **Insights** on each post after a few days. Note which posts got the most saves, shares and messages, not only likes. Saves and messages show real interest, and those are the post types to make more of.
Only post true claims
Never claim a product cures a disease or is "NAFDAC approved" unless it has a real NAFDAC registration number. False claims can lead to complaints, account reports and legal trouble.

You do not need an expensive camera to make good video. Modern smartphones record sharp video. What makes most phone video look poor is not the phone but **shaky hands, bad light, a dirty lens and messy sound**. Fix those four and your video will look far more professional. This lesson covers the camera side; sound is covered in Lesson 3.4.
A movie camera
Your phone is a capable video camera once you control light and steadiness.
Before you press record
**Clean the lens** with a soft cloth. A greasy fingerprint makes everything look hazy, and it is the most common cause of soft, foggy footage.
**Check storage and battery.** One minute of 1080p video can take roughly 100 MB or more depending on the phone, and 4K takes much more. Clear space first.
**Turn on gridlines** in camera settings. They divide the screen into nine boxes and help you keep the horizon level and place your subject.

**Choose resolution and frame rate.** For social media, **1080p at 30 frames per second (fps)** is a sensible default: sharp enough, smaller files, less data to upload. Use 4K only if you have storage and a reason.
**Switch on airplane mode or Do Not Disturb** so a call does not interrupt a good take.
Vertical or horizontal?

Shoot **vertical (9:16)** for Reels, TikTok, YouTube Shorts, Stories and WhatsApp Status. Shoot **horizontal (16:9)** for standard YouTube videos and anything shown on a TV or projector. Decide before you start, because cropping later loses quality and can cut off people's heads.
Focus and exposure

Phones adjust focus and brightness automatically, which can cause the picture to pulse lighter and darker as you move. Tap on your subject's face to focus. On iPhone, press and hold to lock focus and exposure (AE/AF Lock appears). On most Android phones, tap the subject and a lock or a sun slider appears. Slide the sun icon down slightly if bright areas, such as a white wall or the sky, are losing detail.
Light: the biggest free upgrade
Face a window with daylight falling on your face. Do not stand with the window behind you, or you become a dark shape.
Avoid harsh midday sun directly overhead, which makes dark shadows under the eyes. Shade or early morning and late afternoon light is softer.
Turn off mixed lights: a yellow bulb plus blue daylight gives strange skin colours.
A cheap ring light helps at night, but place it in front of you at eye level, slightly above.
Steady shots

Shaky video is tiring to watch. Hold the phone with both hands and tuck your elbows against your body. Walk slowly with bent knees if you must move. Better still, use a phone tripod or rest the phone against books on a table. Many phones also have video stabilisation; leave it on. Use the main (1x) lens for the best quality; digital zoom beyond the phone's optical lenses makes the picture soft. If you need to be closer, walk closer.

Medium: show the action
Close-up: show the detail

A **shot list** is a short plan of each clip you need. Professional editors cut between different shot sizes to keep video interesting. A **wide shot** shows the whole scene, a **medium shot** shows a person from the waist up or hands working, and a **close-up** shows a detail, such as a stitch or a sauce bubbling. Record each clip for at least 5 to 10 seconds so you have room to trim.

Script structure: Hook, Value, Action
**Hook (0 to 3 seconds)**: a strong first image and line. "Stop wasting your tomatoes", "This is how we pack 100 orders a day", or show the finished result first.
**Value (middle)**: the tip, the steps, the transformation or the story. One idea only.
**Action (last 3 to 5 seconds)**: what to do now. Follow for more, send a message, visit the shop.

Write the script in short spoken lines, as you would talk to a friend. Read it aloud and time it. About 2 to 3 spoken words per second is a natural pace, so a 30-second video holds roughly 60 to 80 words of speech.
Repeatable formats
Instead of inventing something new every day, choose two or three formats you can repeat. Repeating formats makes production faster and helps your audience know what to expect.
**Process video**: show how you make or prepare something (sewing a dress, baking, packing an order).
**Before and after**: a hairstyle, a cleaned shoe, a decorated hall. (Do not use before and after for weight loss or skin treatment claims.)
**Quick tip**: one useful tip linked to your product (how to store shea butter in hot weather).
**Customer question answered**: read a real question and answer it in 20 seconds.

Photos are the backbone of your content: products, food, finished work, team and customers. Good light is the biggest difference between a dull photo and a professional one, and the best light is free: **daylight**. In this lesson you learn to find and use natural light, compose photos, and edit them lightly on your phone.
A camera with flash

Understanding natural light

**Window light**: place your subject beside a window, with light coming from the side. This gives soft, shaped light. Avoid windows with direct sun streaming in, or cover them with a thin white curtain to soften it.
**Open shade**: outdoors, stand in the shade of a building or tree, facing the open sky. Skin looks even, with no harsh shadows.
**Golden hour**: the first hour after sunrise and the last hour before sunset give warm, soft light, lovely for portraits and outdoor products.
**Avoid midday overhead sun**: it creates dark eye shadows and shiny spots.
**Avoid the phone flash** for most business photos; it flattens the subject and causes harsh shadows and red eyes.

A **reflector** bounces light back into shadows. You do not need to buy one: a sheet of white cardboard, a white bedsheet or even aluminium foil on card, held on the side opposite the window, lifts dark shadows.
Composition basics
**Rule of thirds**: turn on gridlines and place your subject on one of the lines or where two lines cross, not always in the dead centre.
**Clean background**: remove clutter. A plain wall, a cloth, or a wooden board makes the product stand out.
**Fill the frame**: walk closer instead of using digital zoom.
**Angles**: shoot flat items such as plated food or fabrics from directly above; shoot tall items such as bottles and bags straight on at their own height; shoot people at eye level.
**Leading lines**: roads, tables and shelves can guide the eye towards the subject.

**Copyright** protects photos, music, videos, designs and writing from the moment they are created. In Nigeria, copyright is governed by the Copyright Act 2022 and administered by the Nigerian Copyright Commission. Creative Commons in brief

**Creative Commons (CC)** licences let creators share work with clear conditions. **BY** means you must credit the creator. **SA** (ShareAlike) means your new work must use the same licence. **NC** (NonCommercial) means no business use. **ND** (NoDerivatives) means you may not change it. **CC0** means the creator has given up rights, so you may use it freely. For a business post, avoid NC images. A good credit looks like: "Photo: Name, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons".

Copyright also covers music and video. Using a popular song in a business video, or reposting someone else's video without permission, can get your post muted or removed. Reposting with credit is not the same as permission; ask the creator first and keep their written reply.
